column1: # What this project asks reality, seeded by felix new.
# Felix may declare which question to ask. Felix may never author the answer.
# Each row names a predicate and the command that enumerates its members; the
# members come back from the command, and nothing in the engine can add one.
# predicate
#   predicate  what is being established. A noun, not a verdict.
#   grounds    the capability this supplies ground truth for, or `-`. This is
#              what lets `felix probes` report a surface the checkout has and
#              nothing reads.
#   when       a command deciding whether this row applies here. Exit 1 means
#              not-applicable, which is silent and claims nothing; any other
#              non-zero is unknown, which blocks. `-` = always.
#   probe      the enumerating command. One member per line on stdout.
#   witness    an INDEPENDENT command that exits 0 when the surface exists and
#              1 when it does not. Any other exit is neither, and blocks.
# The witness is the only thing that separates "there is nothing here" from "I
# cannot see", so a row without one can never report `empty` and always blocks
# as `unknown`. That is deliberate and it is the point of the whole table: on
# five occasions a check reported clean because it found nothing, and the last
# of them printed "All gates passed" while naming four unlimited services.
# Make the witness genuinely independent. A witness that re-runs the probe
# agrees with it by construction, which buys nothing — the same defect as a
# fixture that builds only the shapes the rule already names.
# And make sure its EXIT STATUS answers the question. The seeded `test_file`
# witness here first read `ls -d test tests spec __tests__ 2>/dev/null | head -1`,
# whose status is head's — zero, whatever ls found. It said "this surface
# exists" about every repository on earth, so a project with no tests was born
# `blind` rather than `empty`. That is this table's own failure class inside its
# own template: a verdict taken from the last stage of a pipeline instead of
# from the question. End a witness in `grep -q .`, not in `head`.
# And make sure it proves the SURFACE, not its container. The seeded
# `tracked_file` witness was `test -e .git`, which proves a repository exists
# and nothing about whether it tracks a file — so a project created on a fresh
# `git init` with no commit read `blind` and its first gate went red. The last
# commit's tree (`git ls-tree -r HEAD`) is what proves files are tracked, and
# it is independent of the index the probe reads.
# START THE PROBE WITH A BARE COMMAND NAME WHERE YOU CAN. The instrument that
# answered is derived from the first word — `git ls-files` records git and a
# token that changes when git is replaced, so a count that moves because the
# tool moved can be told apart from one that moves because the tree did. A probe
# beginning with an assignment, a variable or a subshell records no instrument,
# which is honest and is also less than you could have had. `felix probes` says
# how many rows are in that state.
# It is only ever the OUTERMOST command, so `python -c "import x; ..."` records
# python and not x. Where that matters, the report saying "identifies no
# instrument" is more useful than a name that tracks the wrong thing.
# Rows run in the checkout being examined, as shell. They are founder-authored
# and live in an enforcing table: shrinking this file escapes to a person.
# Seeded rows below read what git and the filesystem already know, so no row
# here is a new idea. Delete what does not apply and add what does.
tracked_file
test_file
ci_workflow
